blocks.x: So it's all going right now. So you can start off with your name, I guess.

My name is Clem Raymond. My age is 65. I live downtown, San Bernard and Durginwa Street, New Orleans. My first instruction was Papa Teal. Later, I move uptown, Cater's and Liberty Street, and I start taking lessons with old man Umfrey. Later in years, I left New Orleans to New York. I was working for the United Fruit Company Boat Company. There I met a bunch of boys from New Orleans by the name of the Johnson Brothers, which encouraged me to leave the boat and work as music. And that's the encouragement I had coming to California. I continued to work as a chauffeur and whatnot. And in my music career, I began working with a lady from New Orleans by the name of Alma Hightower, the name of the Johnson Brothers, which was a great inspiration in music for me, which helped to build up my career in reading ability. stuff with stuff Later we formed a band and went to Tier 1 of the White for George Montgomery, the owner. And it was at the main event and the main attraction was Jack Johnson which remained there for more than eight months. Later I was connected with Jelly Roll Martin from New Orleans and the band was called The Incomparable New Orleans Jazz Band by Jelly Roll Martin. And for more than two years I played with him all of his original numbers and many standards. Some of my associates at home, Piana was Arthur Campbell, Clarence Tard, to my knowledge were not known as myself at home. Clarence, Friends or Johnny Dot, Wade Whaley, they were not known. Peter Brown, Laurent LaRue, not known. Cut.
I was going to ask first of all the exact birth date, when your birth date is?
February the 6th, 1894.
What part of town were you born in you told?
Saint Bernard and Dujuan, the French part of town.
Just downtown? Yes. Did any of your parents play any instruments?
My father did. He played an accordion, played by air.
Had he played in any bands?
Oh no, no. Just took it up as a hobby, that's all. Everyone worked for a living.
Did you have any brothers or sisters that played any instruments?
No, no brother or sister.
And I wonder too, I know of course you started on clarinet, but was there any other instrument you played a little bit before that?
I tried to play piano, but it didn't do good or wasn't successful. It seemed like my associates were the ones that I was visiting. Everyone was crazy about a clarinet, so I took a liking to it.
About how old were you? When I started? When you got your clarinet.
Oh, it was given to me by my grand-aad. I think I was 14 years old.
And you ever played around those little canon flutes, you know, like they have some of the kids played?
Oh yes, I played that and they had another thing they called a juice hop and I played a mouth hop, a French hop they used to call it. Harmonica something you called it. Yeah, harmonica, yeah.
So I wondered what music you first heard when you were young, if there was something in your home like your father, or would you hear parades or bands playing around the neighborhood?

Oh, my father. No, he always had an accordion. And during my childhood time, as far as I can remember, that when they would have these house parties, why they'd get him to play for us. So naturally I would go along with him too.
Was it sort of dance music?
Oh yeah, he played dance music, yeah. They had old tunes as a, let's see what they called them at that time. I can't think of the name of it.
Do you remember any of the quadrilles?
Yeah, that's what they were, quadrilles, yeah.
Did he play other things like more of the folk music and blues or anything of that kind?

No, during that time in my childhood there wasn't so much blues. It was mostly called ragtime. They didn't play that, it was all quadrilles. No. Because they had one guy who would be over there howling the dance and they'd go around the floor to take the beds down, you know, the great big rooms.
They'd have those dances right in their home then?
Yeah, right in the home, not in no dance hall, no right in the home.
Do you remember any parades when you were a kid? The brass bands?
Oh yes, I remember the parade very well.
Do you remember which bands they were or did you follow any of those musicians? Certain ones that you liked when you were a kid that were your idols you might say and you tried to follow them more?

Well, I followed the parade true enough, yes, because it's King Oliver, he played and so did Ory. He had a band in Celestan and those are the three bands that mostly got the funeral parades to my knowledge.
Can you remember the clarinet players in there, who they were that you...
I had Big Eye Louie and Bessier. Let's see, who else?
Bocquet.
Well, yeah, later Johnny Dodd did play a couple of funerals, I do remember that.
Do you remember George Bocquet when you were young, hearing him?
I remember Charlie Bocquet. Do you know him?
No, no, I only, I met George was the only one I ever knew.
Charlie was a trumpet player wasn't he? Charlie called it? Charlie Bocquet.

Charlie Bocquet. You had another brother who played clarinet didn't he? Iseal. Iseal Bocquet. Somebody told us about another brother too, that you once said you didn't remember him. I don't know who that was. Do you remember some of them? Little Bocquet? Mm-hmm. Talked like you had another third brother. I mean, there were three of them. But do you remember the Teos? Did you tell us something about the Papa Teo was your teacher?
Yes, he was. He was a wonderful old man.
I think it happened to go to him.

I was living near down there, San Bernard and Durjan War. He's a little bit more towards Canal Street. And I know his son, Lorenda, because he played a C clarinet. And he was the only one who had a job that if he did lay it off, that I had a chance to go and play for a dollar and a half. I did play a few jobs before I left New Orleans, but no record of those things, see.
Yeah. I wondered, which church did you belong to? Did you hear any special music in the churches? Were you Catholic or Protestant?

No, I was Methodist at that time. That's a good point you brought up because, to my knowledge, most all the musicians have some faith in my grandfather as a minister. You were the minister? Yes. Mm-hmm.
Do you remember any of the music in the churches when you were a boy?

Oh, yes. In my school they still sing. I'm now in the churches. Same standard church number. But the numbers of bands are playing nowadays, why they wasn't using them during those times. Yeah. Mm-hmm. I attended New Orleans University.
Oh, yes. At Penesbury, right? Yes. That's the one up on St. Charles? That's right. You went way up to that? Yeah.

Well, they didn't have to pay for me to go to school because my grandfather was a minister, so I ain't got it bad. Oh, I see. Is that a Methodist school? Yeah, that's a Methodist. You are a Methodist person?
Yeah. Yeah. That's a Methodist school, since y'all have been on T. Yeah.
How old were you when you left New Orleans? About? Sixteen.
Sixteen.
You did play a few dances then?
Well, we call them dances, yes. I didn't get paid for it, but I went and played anyway. It's just how I didn't get to play.
Do you remember the other musicians that were in the band?
Well, they had a drum and a piano and clarinet. That was all. There wasn't no bands then.
Do you remember the other fellows? There were any of them?

I can't recall the piano player now. How I got to play it, Pete Lawless was through larynge. He was sick. They wanted somebody, because I guess I was taking lessons from his father. I couldn't play near as good as he could. Because he had the C clarinet and he played all the melody. And I didn't, never learn to play strictly melody. Yeah. Can you tell me just what Catello taught you? That is, what kind of a book, can you remember what kind of a book you had? What kind of exercises or what he made you do? And you went there for a lesson. to see clarinet and he played all the melody and I didn't never learn to play strictly melody see
played the original New Orleans star can you tell me just what the CTO taught you that is what kind of a book can you remember what kind of a book you had what kind of exercises or what he

made you do when you went there on the for a lesson oh yeah I bought a method the method cost a dollar quarter at that time and I'm trying to think of the name of it now if I can and you start in the beginning of the book where you have your whole notes quarter notes and as you advance and you have two parts one foot for two clarinets and so on did he start you right with the instrument
oh yes I had a little bit in the air training or something or reading music first before he let

you pick up the instrument or no I had an instrument before I went to him yeah you've been playing a little bit on the play that what I could yes and in school I had music before I went to him I knew notes yeah but no instrument when I was in school yeah they would give you music on the blackboard I knew the note but I didn't know the vision so well no I had music before I got the instrument when I went to him I had the instrument oh by the way I guess it was an Albert system I still have it when I was in the service they issued me a band and I couldn't play it and I still have an Albert when you cut that I'll show it to you and I had in the room I intended to bring it in here

oh yeah we'll talk about that later when we get it out here yeah but I'd still like to hear more a little bit more about your lessons with the about T.O. what kind of a teacher was he was he real strict or did he did he another thing did he ever play with you did he ever have his clarinet there or did he just

oh yeah he used his clarinet because he showed me how to make different passages and then he would play something and say well boy you do this way you do that way and so on well I wasn't that far advanced and if I didn't go I had to pay the 25 cents for the lesson just to see charge 25 cents a lesson well that was a lot of money that's right yeah there's a day she got her quarters where you go well that's that's what I paid 25 cents a lesson and by moving around and working all the time you want to cut it no that's right no that's right everything and I went uptown the same way and a lot of time well Mr. Humphrey was different I was just across the street from him and if I couldn't go and have to work I was a chauffeur during that time and he wouldn't charge me nothing you moved uptown then? yeah I got a job uptown it was too far to travel my auntie was living uptown so that's when I live up then I started taking lessons with him
yeah where did he live about? I never did know
Cated and Liberty Street Cated? C-A-D-I-Z Cated and Liberty right on the corner I would say the downtown back that's right some of his boys still live up in that neighborhood
yeah some of them out here in Los Angeles well let's see Willie do you know the young clarinetist Willie and
no I knew I knew the old man see he's along my age that's right yeah and then his younger kids come up another Willie
yeah that's right his son Willie still live
yeah I don't know that I don't know his children
didn't know the Grand Noob no that's right I guess he wouldn't know that
They all live uptown there yet, and Willie Umphrey, the one you did know, the boy that played clarinet, he had a stroke.
He did.
He's in a wheelchair now. Can you imagine that? We'll go around and take care of him, but he looks well, he looks healthy and big and strong, and his legs are gone. He's seven and nine now.

Old man Jim? No, Willie. What is his father? Willie Umphrey? Willie Umphrey? Yeah, his name Willie Umphrey Jr. I suppose, yeah. Younger's father. Well, I don't know of him, see. I didn't know, I thought it was his father.
No? No, I saw him last spring sometime. 79. What did Mr. Umphrey teach you? Did he keep on with the same book, or did he have you doing the other things?

Well, that's because, uh, it was a cola book, it was, about that thick. Oh, yeah. Yeah, and they had all type of exercise. I never did complete the book by going from place to place and working here and working there. So, they would mark up my next lesson and I'd practice on that when I could. It just was a hazard. It wasn't like things are now, the days where people can take time. I still had to work. So, there was a skip here and there, here and there.
I was gonna ask if all of your teachers then, if they taught by having your teeth on the mouthpiece, or did any of them have you cover your upper teeth too?
I think I gained that knowledge from being around other clarinet players or musicians. No, when I first went, I used the lip, no teeth.
That's right, the lip was right.
No teeth.
Then you later changed. To what? You put your upper teeth on there, Ralph? No, not at all.
You put both lips on. That's right. The method book tells you. Yeah. The teeth should guide on the mouthpiece.
Yeah, a lot of those method books do.

But when you do that, certain times, vibration makes around the orchard. Where you see clarinet players, they have them capped and all that. But the vibration teeth that mount. One time you say, I was clarinet's wooden mouthpiece, it used to bite like an axe. I see them cut right through. You saw our shit. Yeah, that's right. I've seen them, yeah. You see, I'm due to tricking me that iron, yeah. I was using a lip like that.
That all. Yeah, do you remember this old man T.O., did he ever teach you that way or how did he teach you?

The most experience he was teaching me about raising my fingers so high and to get enough breath to make a passage without breaking it. Yeah. If I can break it down to you, you can see the sense in it. When I first went for a lesson, I could play what I could hear but I couldn't read it. I think that helped me some. No, that was, I know how to do everything but I wanted to learn to read the music. So that was my problem and what I was interested in. You know, I knew everything, how to hold the instrument and whatnot. But he said, oh, a ray's too high, you can't get back fast enough. Well, I never did learn to do that properly but after getting good on it, it didn't seem to make any difference. Whatever I was going to make, I could get back just the same.
I just wondered if old Papa T.O. had ever mentioned, told you to put your teeth on or told you to cover your lips or how he taught it.

Well, he would look at me and say, that's right and then he'd walk around and for an instant he might go to the kitchen there and say, that's not right. I didn't know I'd missed a note and he'd come back and he could tell me what note I missed. No, he was very good. I think everyone would recommend him. In other words, during my time, he was considered the best clarinetist down there.
Yeah, but T.O. wasn't always famous, I know.
Yeah, well, I didn't know him to play when I got acquainted with him and started. That's all he was doing, teaching. Yeah. And you'd have to pay him whether you come or not. He had that system.
You went to his home. Do you remember where he lived?

I can't remember that street so well. That's been a long time, 40, 40 times. He lived down below Dumain, the street next to Dumain Street. Yeah, they would call the name of it. What up? This is Humain and then there's St. Philip. He lived down on St. Philip and Murray, rather than that. And Robinson or Murray. Yeah. Not Robinson. Yeah. Philip, yeah.
Well, there's some of the Billary is back there and then Claver. He didn't play there.
Yeah. Well, Billary, he didn't live on Billary. He lived right next street to Dumain Street. Not just like Dumain. Yeah, probably St. Philip. Yeah. Right in that section.
Yeah, they call that the Creole section. Oh, yeah.
Yeah.
Did he talk Creole sometimes to you or did he usually?
No, he didn't, but I could understand a little bit because my father couldn't talk English. Was he French?
Yeah.
You were a French family, huh?
Yeah.
My father was on my mother's side. Yeah.
When you first came to California, do you remember about what year was there or did you go on the road first? You said to New York someplace before you came here?

No, out of school, yes. I worked for the United Fruit Company boat. Oh, yeah. Yeah. And that's how I got to New York. So, I got with those Johnson boys, as I said. Let's see, one was a guitar player and the other was a bass player. Did you know them? The Johnsons?

Well, there's so many Johnsons. Is that Bill Johnson, you think? No, no, no, no. Wasn't that bunch? No, Bill Johnson from Monk. From out here. The bass player, yeah. He was out here already. That's why I remember him.
Johnson. He was at Dunbar's Tennessee Tanks, too. Well, yeah, that's when I got out here, but I didn't go back, see?
When did you first come to California?
1915 when they had the bass here.
1915 you came here? Yeah. Somebody told me the other day they thought you came here in 1912, but that wasn't right.
Oh, no.
Yeah, somebody told me the other day, I don't know who it was, it doesn't make any difference, but you've been here ever since 1912. No, they got to mix up.

I came here in 1915, and I didn't go back with them. I lived in Los Angeles all that time. Then when I got discharged here in San Francisco, I had a job over here, they used to call it the Barber Coast. Now they call it the International. Yeah. So I worked over there with another old guy from New Orleans. He never did go back. He might have left there in 1912. His name is Sid Leprotti.
Oh, yeah. Did Sid Leprotti come from New Orleans? That's his hometown.
It was his hometown.
Yeah.
Yeah. But he worked all over, and during the war, he was in Australia. So the whole band enlisted in Australia as a band, so they didn't have to go and fight.
And you worked at Sid Leprotti, huh?
When I got discharged, yeah.
I'd hoped to be able to talk to him, but they say he's had several strokes.
I just was out there Friday and couldn't see him. No, he won't come.
Do you think he'll ever recover now? No.
16 strokes. I don't think he'll make it. He don't know nobody. Really?
He's that bad? Mm-hmm.

Mm-hmm. Do you remember, since he won't be able to talk for himself, can you remember a little bit about his life? Did he ever tell you anything? Where he came, just what part of town? Well, no. Did he ever play with or anything?

No, he was very clandestine. In his younger days, you thought maybe he was white. Mm-hmm. So he carried himself that way, and he always seemed to bend in the money or something. So I never did visit his home and never was that close.
Never did get to hear much about his life?
No.

No. There's one friend of mine once had a little homemade recording of him. I think they took on the job once, so I did get to hear him play Four O'Clock Blues, and I think he played The Pearls, that piece of jelly roll.
Yeah. And he had one number of his own that he used to play all the time, but he sold a copyright. It's called Canadian Capers. Oh, that was his number?
Originally, yeah.
Oh, really?
I never knew that. Mm-hmm.
Mm-hmm. And he sold it so he can't make any claim for it anymore.
Yeah. And he did compose that?
Yeah. He and this fellow, Gerald Wells, he's 72. He lived in Seattle. He quit music altogether, too. He's in the real estate business.
Is he from New Orleans by any chance?
Who, Gerald Wells? Mm-hmm. No, he's a West Indy.

West Indy. Mm-hmm. I wasn't sure Sip, but it probably came from New Orleans, and you're sure of that then? Yeah. He didn't come from his barn down that way. Yeah. Came out here real early and worked at the Barbary Coast.

Yeah, well, he worked all over. Yeah. And that's why I said he could have been here, or up in Canada, or somewhere. The band was called So Different. Mm-hmm. And I had the Spike Brothers and... I'll tell you last night. Mm-hmm. The Black and Tam Band, and they and themselves were so different. Did I tell you that? No, I don't remember who the Black and Tam? Yeah, they and themselves were so different. And the SIDS Band was so different, because they had Slocum Williams. He's from New Iberia, Slocum. He's dead. He was a clarinet player. He was a clarinet player.
Mm-hmm.
There was only six of them.
You know, Dick Johnson recorded a piece for me once. I may put out some records of it years ago. I think for many years.
He's some kind of Jellie Roll.

Yeah, his brother-in-law. Mm-hmm. And Dick, one piece he played, sort of the slow blues. And I said, what's the name of that? He said, well, call it the So Different Blues. And I thought that was a funny name, but I never know it came from the band. I wondered where he got that. He never didn't mean much to me.

Well, I was out there in 1919. Who? I said, well, I was out there in 1919. Yeah. They called it Band of So Different Band. Mm-hmm. They all died out there, folks. Yeah, both of the Spike brothers dead. Slocum's dead. Cheryl Green, he's dead? Yeah. And Doc was the drummer. He got killed in the tube over there, Stockton Tunnel, rather. They all was dead, and Sid's the only one left. And he's about to pass. How's that fight? How's that? Harris Sutherland, he's living? Who? Harris Sutherland. Oh, no, Harris wasn't dead. He's the one who had the black and tan band in love. And that band, yeah. Yeah, he's the barber. Uh-huh. And how about Minnie? Who? Well, we called Minnie out here. He came out here and he called his man. What do you mean? Ernest Johnson. Oh, Ernest Johnson. His name was Ernest... Craycart. Craycart. Yeah. Where is he? He died, too. Yeah, he's dead, too. Paul Howard, the saxophone player, is the only one living now. And he conducts the Masonic Band and the Elf Band. And the Cali player, the saxophone. And so we talked to... Don't get that recorded wrong there. Howard is nothing, no conductor, nothing. See, I get all that music you see down in my basement comes from the conductor of the Los Angeles Band, the Elf and all the other bands down there. So you think Howard isn't active in music? Howard is active. He's manager's band. He's still has the business. But F.M. Lacey is the conductor of both bands. Oh, well, I had it wrong. I know he was affiliated. He snapped on my music and I hear from Lacey each week. He's a conductor of both bands. Oh, well, I had it wrong. I know he was affiliated. He snapped on my music and I hear from Lacey each week. Lacey writes me. He's my good friend. I talked to Paul Howard.
You know, we tried to find out where Wade Whaley was. And nobody down there knew Paul Howard thought he was up this way. Maybe he said try San Jose.

Yeah, when he left here he went to San Jose. And the next time I heard he went to San Diego. Because I was down in Los Angeles. I was told that he had a little cigar stand and whatnot. And I went all up and down Central Avenue. And nobody knew nothing about him.
We couldn't find any trace of him there. No. Orie the other night when we talked to Orie on the phone said that he thought he, I believe he said he'd seen him in San Diego and he played down there.

I think you're wrong. You might have seen him down there. Just a little small town. He's not far from here. Might be around. But I've been looking at him. You know your friend, the drummer that comes to see you all the time. The trumpet player, them two boys that just play in your band. Yeah. And you haven't told him about your big band here nor showing him the picture of it. Oh we'll get to that in a minute. Well we'll see if I heard it. I was going to start talking about something. I don't think it was. Yeah, that's all right. Sure, anything you want to talk about is all right. So I was going to ask you then when you came out here, when you first started working, was with Sid to the Prod? Or was it some other group?
When I first started working. When I first started working.
Out here in California. You know your friend, the drummer that comes to see you all the time. Yeah.

You know your friend, the drummer that comes to see you all the time. Yeah. The trumpet player and the two boys that just play in your band. Yeah. And you haven't told him about your big band here nor showing him the picture of it. Well we'll get to that in a minute. Well we'll get to that in a minute. Well we'll get to that in a minute. Well we'll see.

We'll see. We'll see. About stuff I didn't know, I thought she was from Denver. Anyway, she's on the directing board. I saw her. And now I'm from Dallas. Yeah. That Faye's a wonderful gal. She's highly country. She brought me right along, that music deal.
How long did you live down in Los Angeles then? From 1915, you say you moved out about.
Yes. And then, let's see, in 1918, I was drafted in World War I. Went to France, and when I come back is when I started working with Sid. And I left. After that? Yes.
A little bit about your Army experience. You said you...
You had trouble with that bane system clarinet.
Well, the Army issued me a bane. So I couldn't play a bane, so I had to carry two clarinet. I had my own, yeah.
So you used your old albert then?
Yes, but I was charged with a bane. So I had to carry a long two clarinet.

What is your opinion of the difference of the two? Is there much difference in tone? Why do you like the albert? Of course you learned on that, so it's easier for you. But if you had your choice to start on either one of them, which would you pick now?

Well, I noticed that so many clarinet players that I found in the albert and I looked at them, the boar in the albert is much larger than the boar in the bane clarinet. And there's more volume. I can get more volume. I can play just another clarinet player and you can't hardly hear them. Well, Dixieland music, like when this band from New Orleans was out here, this George Lewis band, they play awful strong.
Yeah, they do.
Well, I could be heard with them.
He played with them. I know, yeah. Darman Pierce told me about it. Yeah.
So that's the difference I find.

Do you think you can do more with it? That is, the clarinet, by not having as many keys, does it seem more like it's a part of you that is your fingering? Is there much difference in your fingering? It's the difference in the fingering, yes.
That's what I found. You've never played the bane enough, I guess,
to really get used to it. No, no, I couldn't make it.
To feel how it would feel to play it.
Mm-hmm.
And after I figured I got up in the eight and then the music business got slow and I had to go to work again, I said, well, no need to try and switch. And I'll just stay on that.
Well, you were showing us your clarinet. Yeah.
And you look through it in the light, the bore that drilled the hole in there, see how big that hole. Oh, yeah, it's really a big bore. Well, it's much bigger than the buffet.
What make is this?
That's a buffet. This is it.
This is it.
Yeah, it was the medical system. Do you see the difference, Mr. Roussel? The road hand on the bell. Do you see the difference in that,

Liz Buffett and my Buffett? I don't know. No, I don't remember. Why? I don't know. I've never had yours in my hand very much. Once you see it, it's all right. Does this have more keys than yours? No, I say oh my. Do you see it? No. It's straight, a little piece like a... Oh, sure, yeah.
Why didn't I see that? Yeah. The minus giants in that. It doesn't come apart yet. Keep it all in one long piece. Yeah, the case is like a violin case.
Yeah. Raymond Burke has one like that,
both an A and a B-flat, all in one piece. Big long case.
Yeah, I never even said it. That's improved.
It must be improved. I've never made them like that before. Three keys down here.
Yeah, look at your... Yeah, that key feels like it's up sort of high though, do you think? Oh, so you have it up there then? Yeah, that's right. Yeah.

About stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff stuff Well, I don't have to use the others.
You don't have to use a bunch anyway.
No, just use that big one for C-sharp. And that other one on the outside of C-sharp, the E-flat, I never have to go over there for it.
Is this the same instrument you had in the Army and carried all that time?
No, I just told him that's the third one I had in California.
Third one you got out there.
Yeah.
Yeah, I guess you call that an improved, Albert.

It was improved for the ones I had. It didn't have no keys or no rolls or nothing. But I always used a buffet because that's what Papa Teal had. The clarinet players there, if you didn't have a buffet, you didn't have no clarinet.

What kind of fest has gotten? You say George Barquet got yours fest for you? Yeah, Malcolm, Alfred Wilson. Oh, yeah, piano player. I'm always going to ask what kind of a reed you use. Do you use a stiff reed or medium or soft? What kind of a reed do you like?

Well, since I don't play so often, I use a number three. They call that almost medium. Yeah, number three. And then when I play band music, I have what they call a plastic reed. It's a number four. It don't become water soap. It changes the tone. You don't get a sweeter tone or a soft tone like you would. So playing street music, you want to hear the clarinet. And most of the clarinet players around here, they're used to sitting down and play, and they can't walk in place. So I try to help out. But I play strong. But other than that, I use a number three.
Did you ever play any parades as much on the street? And, of course, not the New Orleans. I guess you left there too soon.
Yeah. But here, occasionally, we had parades, yeah. Because during my...
Why didn't you have...

Well, not only that. Before we had trouble out here with this Harriet Bridget, whatever, Labor Day, I would control, not say control, he would give me the job for three bands, so I would split them up. And Mr. White would help me in conducting and arranging the bands, so I would have 20 men in each section. So I would hire 60 musicians or more. A local six would have six musicians. So I'd done quite a bit of street work.
Yeah. Did you ever play an E-flat clarinet in any of this?
No, I never did, no.
Did you ever have both an A and a B-flat clarinet on any jobs, or just always transpose or play everything on the B-flat?
Well, at one time in 1919, I had an A clarinet, and I quit writing music for A clarinet.
Most of the dance bands.
Yeah, and they all had B-flat, so they'd not gotten rid of it. So nowadays, they don't use nothing but B-flat.
Well, can you tell us, then, when you joined, after the war, you joined Sid Leprotti's band. How do you pronounce that, Leprotti?
Yes. That's L-A-P-R-O-T-T-I. Aye. That's a French name, Leprotti. The name is Sidney, and they call him Sid.
And he was the leader of the band.

That's right, yeah. And I was waiting for my disjoint, and I used to go down there every night when I'd get out of camp, sit up there and play for nothing. But they said, well, I'll give you a job after you get out of here. So I accepted for a while.
Where did you work? What sort of a job was it? In the dance hall?
Oh, no. During that time, it was called a cabaret. It was called them cabarets during that.
Do you remember which one?

Oh, yeah. The man is dead now. His name was Lester Mapp. But the time Sid started to work in this particular place at Kernan Jackson Street, there was another West Indian on the place by the name of Lou Purcell. And he died, and he turned it over to Lester Mapp. They both were West Indian. But Lester was working for Lou. So Sid just continued to stay there. It was at Kernan Jackson Street, San Francisco.
It was really almost part of the old Barbary Coast. It was. It was. Yes. Some Alabama, too.
Yeah, well, that's out in the Fillmore District. That all originated later.
Can you tell me about when Jelly Roll came out here, or was he already here when you got here?

He was here when I got here. In 1915? Yeah. I don't know when he'd come here, because I've been reading other histories. Well, he was in Kansas City and around Chicago and New York, but I remember him being here when I came here in 1915.
In San Francisco or Los Angeles?
No, Los Angeles.
Los Angeles.
Yeah.
Remember, was he working or playing music?

Oh, yeah, because he never had no band. As he said in some of his old LPs, the guys that played horns didn't make much money. So he kept busy all the time. He was a whole band by himself. Yeah, he worked every night. And then movie colony down there in Los Angeles. It wasn't calling Hollywood then. Well, they'd come out. The man didn't know when he had a payday coming. He'd come and hand him a $50 bill to play one number. He really cleaned up, but he couldn't keep nothing. Well, most musicians don't.
Oh, yeah, easy come, easy go.
Yeah. And they had him a $50 bill. Another thing I can recall in 1915, that all the paper money from a $10 bill up was all gold money.
Oh, that's right.
Yeah, it was all gold. And they didn't see no silver out at all. Even the other money was gold. They had two and a half gold pieces, five, ten, and twenty.
Out here, they really used that gold then.
Yes, they did.
Five dollar bills, you'd get a five dollar gold piece.
Yeah.
I never remember those.
Not the bill. The bill ran ten and twenty, fifty dollars. The five dollars wasn't gold. I don't recall that. But I mean a little two and a half gold piece, about as big as a quarter.
I've seen the electors.
But like you see silver, if you've ever been up around Nevada, we've never seen no silver around here during those days, no.
All silver.
All gold. Even the paper money was gold. That's what I was trying to say.
Yeah, I guess because they mined gold out here.
Or something, yeah.
Yeah. Did you join Jelly Roll in playing in a band or anything with him ever? Did you ever play with him?

Oh, yes. Yeah, I mentioned that. I was with him for two years when he decided to organize a band. And we went from town to town to play. And we played around Los Angeles and various places. We were, as a band of six of us. We were trying to operate a place. It was called Leakes Lake.
Oh, yeah. That was down in Watts, wasn't it?
That's right, yeah. That's right.
And I went down there. Where was it? Can you remember about what part?
No, I wouldn't remember. I even had papers and everything for that place because I was trying to buy it by paying rent for it. And the rent was, but it wasn't successful.
Well, what was Leakes Lake? Was it really a lake or a resort?
A big pavilion, a big pavilion. See, in any place you wanted to have something like a big gathering, it would go to Leakes Lake. That's the only place available at that time.
Was it really a lake or anything there?

No, a big dry place, but they named it Leakes Lake. And someone told me when it used to rain so hard and everything get flooded, it was like a lake, so they named it Leakes Lake. Oh. But it was a great big pavilion.
Where did you get the Leakes part? Was that the name of the man that owned it or something?
Well, I couldn't recall that either, no.
You know, it's funny. It was a big dance pavilion.
Yeah.
Was there a ground there for picnics and theaters?

Well, yes. No one seemed to keep it up at that time. They had little tables built out there, but no grass or nothing. People would sit out there and have their lunch. And summertime would be so hot around there. They'd sit out and drink beer. They had those tables built on the ground. Yeah. Yeah.
And the Jellies band played out there.
Yeah.
That is what it's called, Incomparables or...
Incomparable.
Incomparables.
Yeah, he named it that. That's the time him and Dink fell out. I'm trying to remember the drummer we had. He wouldn't let Dink play for him no more.
What happened to him?

Well, Dink always come late and Jetta Rola was very temperamental. You know, he had to be there on time. It's all right for him to walk in. Well, I'm the boss. I don't have nothing to do. Boom. He'd stomp on me, there we go. You'd be there on time, ready to play. Dink come there and take him a half an hour to set up his drum. Yeah. I heard he passed.
Yes, about 1954 or several years ago. About four years ago in November, I think. Didn't I? Up in Portland.
Oh, he went to Portland. Yeah. He left Santa Barbara. Yeah.
Right up there. And he'd been down to Santa Barbara. And he also had a place right next to Wrigley Field there when I knew him. A little restaurant.
Yeah.
Called Dink's Place. And musicians, what do you call it? Musicians Club or something. I don't remember. Who else was in the band?
Well, I can recall a saxophone player. And he's dead. His name was Bynum. That's all I can remember. The trumpet player. He was a fucker.
Who was he doing?
He played a tenor sax. And the trumpet player was a fellow after 24th Infantry. He's dead. I can't remember his name. But he wasn't from around New Orleans or nothing.
He came up in Los Angeles.
Yeah. Let's see who. This Woodman. You met him. His son played with Duke Ellerton. He's a barber down there. He was playing trombone.
I know the name. I never remember.
Well, his young son. Well, that's the last name, Woodman. I don't even remember his first name.
He had about five pieces then.
We had six. Six. Was there a bass? Yeah, we had a bass player. But they didn't play a bass like Mount Tutti. No.
You knew Judy then pretty well.
Oh, yeah. I knew him in New Orleans.
Yeah.
We saw him a week ago Saturday night. Had a nice visit with him.
He did, huh?
He looks well. He was working that night, too.
Down south?
Yeah.
Oh, yeah. He was still my friend.
Yeah. He drove his car to work. It was about 9 o'clock. He had to go to work.
80 Garland. Yeah, I remember him.
Yeah. And you worked with Jelly about two years with that family.
Yeah.
Most of your jobs down at Leech Lake?

No, just all over. We worked in several theaters around there. They used to get a little group together in like a vaudeville. You know how you gig. It was mostly gigging. Then he disappeared, and I went back down to Tier 1 and worked for Syl Stewart. Through Jelly Roll, he got me the job. I worked down there just a clarinet and piano.

I remember Dink told me once about one job. He was mad about Jelly. Dink claimed he got the job at a hotel, the richest hotel, I believe, in San Diego. And Jelly would go in and always insist on crossing his legs on each leg. The boss didn't like that and told him not to do it. And Jelly said, well, I crossed my legs in all the best places in Europe and America, I'm going to keep on, and the boss fired him the next night.

Do you remember any of that time? Yeah, I can recall, but I wasn't playing with him. You weren't with him? No, I don't think he had a band. It must have been just he and Dink. Maybe he and Dink. Yeah. They wasn't great for hiring bands then. So Jelly wanted to start something different. Because if I can recall, like in New Orleans, unless they had a dance at St. Ketchum or something, all those jobs down in the district, they only had a clarinet, piano, and a drum, most of them. But when they give a dance where they pay 15 cents or two bits to go in, they would have five or six pieces. Because I used to go to St. Ketchum quite often, even before they started using piano, they used to have a violin play and a guitar, bass fiddle. Well, unless you're playing for a dance, they never had a big band. All those big bands were originated in the later years.
After you left Jelly, you said you went to Tijuana then and played a violin?

Yeah. For Syl Stewart. It was called the Kansas City Bar. That's where he was originated from. They named it the Kansas City Bar. This fellow was named Homer Johnson. I don't know where he came from. He's dead.
Oh, Jelly named a piece called the Kansas City Stump.
Yeah.
After that, I remember he said that...
He had the Kansas City Stump before Syl had the saloon on there. His piece, Kansas City Stump.
He didn't have one called it?
Mm-hmm.
I thought he named it after that place.
No, I remember in his old record he said that, but we were playing Kansas City Stump before...
Before that.

Before Syl had the saloon and named it the Kansas City, because Syl bought it off a Mexican guy and it was called something else. And he named it the Kansas City Bar because he said he was from Kansas City. Yeah.
Remember the other pieces that Jelly played?
Yeah. Mama Anita, he named that after his wife.
Well, that's what I told him once, too.
That's right.
After his wife. She's dead now, too, you know.
She is.
Well, she died about two years ago, I believe.
Oh, I see. I don't know what happened to his royalties now. If we get that.

I don't know. Maybe his sisters are... Anita still has a brother that's up in Portland. In fact, he wrote to me about in June. Oh, I can't remember now his first name. He didn't give me the names. A couple of initials, like R.E. or something. I believe it was. R.E. Johnson. That'd be Robert or something. So, Dink and Bill Johnson is in Texas, I think. He's a bass player, another brother of Anita's. He played with Keppard and Oliver. He played with Oliver a long time. Made records with Joe Oliver in Chicago. And he stayed in Chicago until just four or five years ago. And he's been in Texas and Mexico. But I don't think he's in touch with the rest of the family. So, I don't know what happened to those royalties.
I'll go to someone. Yeah. Next, near his relative, I guess.
Anita was married to, I think the name of Ford, I believe, too.
Yeah.
A place up near on the road up in Oregon. Some place like a roadhouse. Mm-hmm. Was Anita with Jolly in those days then?
Oh, yes.
He traveled and lived with him all the time then?

Well, he didn't travel so much. Not around in that vicinity. So, I don't know whether she went to Chicago when he'd pull up. Because he disappeared. And I don't think anyone knew where he was. At least I did. Mm-hmm. And his favorite piece that he actually put out himself was that Wolverine blues. Oh, yeah. I would like that. He had Kansas City Stomp, but King Porter Stomp. I think he stole that from King Oliver.

Well, I think Jolly said there was a fellow by the name of Porter King. Fess, do you ever remember a Porter King? Oh, King Porter. Well, he said he changed the name around. He called him to King Porter. I know King Porter. Did he call him King Porter? So, I know King Porter. I think that's King Porter. King Porter. I think he said he came from Pensacola. Do you remember? Mm-hmm.
King Porter. Mm-hmm.
Did he play in the district sometime, too? Or around the honky-tonks? Or kind of a pianist? I never saw him around him, Mr. I never saw him.
About to go on.
Yeah.

There were three brothers. One was a tuba player, the other was a piano player. One played a trumpet, and he lost his arms in an accident. And he used to play the black man for him. It's on the floor.

The real, the family name is Porter. Oh, yeah? There was Jolly once on one of those records. He said, I've changed the name around. Basically calling him Porter King. I called him the King Porter. Oh, bright-looking fellas. But his real, the real name is Porter. Porter, yeah. And you said one played piano? I don't know. I played trumpet, and another one.
I know John played trumpet. See, he was on the cold weather side with me. For a while, I was glad he met yesterday, too. Did you ever get any data on William Nicholson? Professor Nicholson?
No, except the fastest over there. He studied piano with him for a while.

Well, he, somewhere, I don't know if you want to cut it off. No, it's all right. He was actually one of the real classic teachers in the audience. That's what Festus did. And his daughter is now Dean of the Department of Music at Wilberforce University. Is that the... Camille Nicholson. That's the daughter of the old professor. That's the daughter of the father. She's an old woman now, for that matter. How much is that now? No. He was... How much is that now? She's at Wilberforce. Huh? She's at Wilberforce in Ohio. Dean of the Department of Music. And she's also... She was president of the Negro Music Teachers Association. I think she's a... She's a vice president or a president emeritus. She is a very, very fine musician. And of course, old man Nicholson was a mighty fine musician. He taught the piano and the violin. Man, he could tell you more about it than my... He took us... Clean... The gal would come out. He's the one that raised the price on music teaching in New Orleans. You couldn't come to him for no 50 cents, no a dollar even. Two. Hmm. One. One. My price. My price. My attorney manual for... $15,000. No, you could come along and... It was way back though, yeah. Yeah. You didn't know him until about 19... 19 or so. I never met him until 1920. I went out to his house to see what he arranged a number for me. He won $25. What is it, Galvis Canal? Yeah. He was off... Off Canal. He was by Galvis and... He was on Galvis. He was between Galvis and Denver. Yeah, that's right. Uh... Iberville. Yeah, Galvis and... Off of Iberville.
You must have studied with him back in 1905 or before, wasn't it, D-Fat? Yeah, he was. You remember when he was teaching me with? Huh?

He was at University. Yeah. I don't remember when he was there. See, when I... He was... He was Professor there. Yeah. When I was at your University. Yeah. Well, I remember... Professor Mamba. Huh? My remembrance of him is just after I got to New Orleans. Oh, yeah. But I had read of it being the orchestra lead on the original Georgia Ministers. And the days when W.C. Handy led the Georgia Ministers band. And that was long before my time. Oh, yeah.
Well, we were talking about... Now, Jelly Roll took some lessons from Professor Nickerson, too. He told... Oh, yeah.
Oh, yeah. I recall in his LP where he used to talk about this woman who used to take lessons from. See, every tune she played was the same thing. Oh, yeah.
Somebody else, yeah.
Yeah. Some woman that was teaching him. Yeah. It's come to find out she couldn't read one note. Yeah.
So... Did Jelly read pretty well when you knew him?

Yes, he could. But he was great for showing off. Well, during his time out here, he was the best piano player. So he didn't fool with no popular numbers. But everything he played with his own numbers, he could give it a name or something. But he could read, yeah. Because when I remember going to a theater, everybody had to read because they had to play. What they call... Some of it was a transcription. And the other was a stock music. So we had to use it for the show. Yeah, he could read.
In Los Angeles, a theater, a diamond.

I don't know if you couldn't read nothing, though. Mm-hmm. Like he spoke about the show. I don't know if you couldn't read nothing. When I just show him, his cause of wine, boy, don't deny my name. That's right. And I'm glad to hear you say that because it's all funny about him being any good reader. He's never no good reader. He criticized his teachers wrongly, too. I was surprised. Yeah, when he made all them trips that got on his feet, composed the numbers. I said, well, he's pretty great. He turned it pretty quick. Well, that's why I thought he stole this number from Joe Oliver, King Porter Stomp. Because I heard Oliver play it. He played it, but I never seen it in music before because it didn't have this Wolverine in music. Everything was jelly roll, jelly roll. That's my number. That's my number. That's how he would... People didn't want to play nothing but his numbers. He'd go to another cafe or cabaret to hear other popular numbers. Just come there to hear and play his numbers.
When did you hear Oliver play that? Before you left New Orleans?
Oh, no. He came out here with the band.
Oh, about that time.
You know he was in San Francisco over there on Market Street. He came from Chicago here.
Yeah, I showed fast where that was. What was it?
Pergola. It's a big market there now, I think.
Right about next to St. Francis Theater.
Yeah, around in there somewhere.
Do you remember Oliver and out here, too? You got to know him and hear the band when they were here?
Oh, yes.
Were you up in San Francisco over that time or down there?

I'd go all over. I always had a car and that's how I used to make my living. I'd go up this far to Portland, Oregon. Just play around, play around and come back down. Then for about nine months, I worked on Market Street. I don't remember the years. It was the Balcony Ballroom when I had 11 pieces over there. So Oliver was out here and that's the time Dodge was with him. They had the drummer Ram. He's still around here somewhere.
I talked to him on the phone in Los Angeles.
He did. In Minor Hall. They call him Ram.
We'll see him when we get back.

Oh, I see. He stood and the rest of the guys went by. That's one of the great numbers. I just thought it was King Oliver's number and they had music to it. So somebody put it down in music. But when Jelly Roll was playing it in Los Angeles, there wasn't no music to it.
Did you all play the Pearls too?
Yeah, that's his. That's one of his. I know that.
That's jolly hard to get along with, would you say? Or is it eccentric, that is? I mean, reliable?

Well, most musicians, I think, being in charge of a group is somewhat temperamental. As I say, he always wants you there on time, but he could come in a few minutes late. Yeah. Naturally, he couldn't say anything. No. But if you late, well, he'd dock it, take it out. It's sound. He was that type of a fellow. That's why he and Dink couldn't get along. You know, Dink used to be the drummer with him. Yeah. And Dink, he tried to organize a little group, but they didn't do no good.
Can you tell about your first experiences when you came up here and played at the Barbary?
About stuff like stuff stuff like stuff stuff like stuff

Matt Wilkerson, he run what they call a cavalry over there, trying to think, Bancroft, that was the name of it. And that was the only two colored spots they had around here in San Francisco. And all the rest of them were white places. And during that time, why local Sikhs were so strong, they said all the territory belongs to them and it was frightening the proprietors from hiring colored musicians. So that's the only two places you had to work. Whereas I said I used to go in and out waiting for my discharge. I was around here about a month before I got discharged. So by going there, sitting up there playing for the tips, he offered me a job. So when I got discharged, I went to Los Angeles, come back up here and work a while.
Can you remember when Sid LaFrawley was up here too? You said you first played with him down the road. In Los Angeles. No, not Sid in Los Angeles.
Oh, you haven't with him?
No, here in San Francisco.
It was here then. That's what I mean.
Yeah, on the Barbara Coast, yeah, San Francisco.
Well, you maybe played with him down there too.
No, I can't recall him being down in Los Angeles.
He came right here then, you think?
Oh, another thing we didn't cover was the Tennessee 10, if Mr. Wright can help you out a little bit. Yes, he can because he can call Slow Kid's name and I can't call it.
Well, Slow Kid had the band, see? He was in charge and through these-
U.S. Thompson. Yeah, Thompson. U.S. Nicknamed Slow Kid Thompson.

That's all I know and could remember if I hadn't forgotten the name. He had the group, it was called the Tennessee 10s and I got acquainted with these two Johnson boys, as I said one was a guitar player and the other was a bass player. So we would close the show on the off him, that's how we come out here.
Where was the band organized or did you just join them?
In New York.
In New York. Were the fellas from the south or Chicago or New Orleans or Tennessee or where were they

coming from? I might say Missouri, but those two Johnson boys were from New Orleans. They had been with them before and I can't remember the clarinet player, it seemed like he got some other job or he didn't want to come with them or something. I used to hang around New York and go to these house rank parties, they used to call them, and play and just got acquainted with them that way. So if I hadn't met them I'd never come out here I don't guess. So that was my first experience trying to actually play music and follow them. So they were versatile, they do a little bit of everything in the closing of the show, more on a minster style.
When you played up here at the Barbary Coast was it with a little band then, a five or six piece band?
Well there were six of us.
Six of us. How long did you work there? It was that same place you're told about?
About with Sid?
With Sid?
Oh about eight months. Then Slocum came down from Canada and he took the job and I went back to Los Angeles.
How long have you been living here in Oakland?
In Oakland? Well, I'd have to think of that. Well you don't want the exact.
Well it doesn't have to be exact. I mean ten years, five years, six, twenty or?
No, I've been up here since about twenty-two, yeah about nineteen-twenty-two. But I would go back and forth, I just didn't... You had about thirty-six years. Uh huh.
Did you ever work with Orie's band?
No, I never did work with Orie.
Did you work with Mutt?
No, Mutt and Orie was together.
They were always together. Yeah. Most of the time I guess. Once or twice they split up, I think, Pops Foster told us yesterday.
Well probably they did, but when they were here working they had this Wade Whaley with them and Orie and Mutt, there was at the Creole Cafe here on Seventh Street.
In Oakland?
Yes.
I never did know where that was. It was right on Seventh Street.
